week_headline: Gut health and dementia prevention dominate headlines this week, with fermented foods, emulsifiers, and antidepressant interactions all sparking debate online

top10.claim: Low - inflammation diet can cut dementia risk by almost 30 %, new study says . Here how
top10.verdict: There is genuine and growing evidence that anti-inflammatory diets — think Mediterranean or MIND-style eating — are associated with lower dementia risk, and some studies do point toward figures in the 20–30% range. But 'cut risk by 30%' is an association finding, not a proven cause-and-effect relationship, and the number shifts depending on how the diet is measured and which population is studied. It's a genuinely promising area, just not a guaranteed protective shield.
sources: JAMA - MIND Diet and Cognitive Decline (Morris et al.)
BMJ - Dietary patterns and dementia risk meta-analysis
NIH National Institute on Aging - Diet and Alzheimer's research overview
top10.global_opinion: In Mediterranean countries like Greece and Italy, this finding barely raises an eyebrow — their traditional diet already aligns closely with anti-inflammatory principles and is widely promoted by national health bodies. In the US, the MIND diet (a hybrid of Mediterranean and DASH) has received dedicated NIH funding and is actively studied at major research universities. In the UK, the NHS acknowledges diet as a modifiable risk factor for dementia but stops short of endorsing specific percentage-based claims, preferring broader healthy eating guidance.
top10.brit_take: Turns out swapping the Friday chippy for more olive oil and leafy greens might actually be doing your future self a favour — though the research isn't quite ready to promise you'll remember where you put your keys.

top10.claim: Study Links Common Food Emulsifiers to Gut Barrier Damage in Healthy Adults – NaturalNews . com
top10.verdict: The concern about emulsifiers isn't invented — some cell and animal studies, and a few human observational studies, do suggest certain emulsifiers like carboxymethylcellulose and polysorbate-80 may affect the gut lining and microbiome at high doses. However, NaturalNews.com is a known source of health sensationalism and the claim of 'gut barrier damage in healthy adults' from a single study overstates what the current evidence actually shows. Regulatory bodies including EFSA and the FDA continue to regard approved emulsifiers as safe at typical dietary exposure levels.
top10.verdict_highlight: Real science, but heavily overstated by the source
sources: EFSA - Re-evaluation of food emulsifiers safety report
Cell - Chassaing et al. emulsifier and microbiome study
BMJ - Ultra-processed food and gut health review
top10.global_opinion: The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) has been conducting rolling re-evaluations of emulsifier safety since 2018 and has issued some cautionary signals on specific additives, leading to tighter scrutiny in the EU than in the US. France has been notably proactive, with researchers at INSERM publishing large cohort studies linking emulsifier intake to inflammatory markers. In the US, the FDA maintains these additives are generally recognised as safe (GRAS), though some scientists argue that GRAS status hasn't been updated to reflect modern gut microbiome research.
top10.brit_take: NaturalNews is about as reliable a health source as your nan's neighbour who 'did their own research' — the underlying science has some merit, but this particular messenger has a habit of turning a molehill into a mountain.

top10.claim: People have been fermenting food for millennia . Here why more people are focused on gut health now
top10.verdict: Fermentation is genuinely one of humanity's oldest food preservation techniques, and the renewed interest in gut health is backed by a rapidly expanding body of microbiome science. A 2021 Stanford study published in Cell showed that a high-fermented-food diet increased microbiome diversity and reduced inflammatory markers — that's meaningful. The nuance is that 'gut health' as a consumer concept has outrun the science considerably, with many probiotic products making claims that aren't yet fully supported by clinical evidence for specific health outcomes.
top10.verdict_highlight: Ancient practice, but commercial claims outrun the science
sources: Cell - Sonnenburg & Gardner fermented food and microbiome diversity study (2021)
Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health - The Microbiome overview
Journal of Nutrition - Probiotic health claims review
WHO - Probiotics in food health and nutritional properties
top10.global_opinion: In Japan and South Korea, fermented foods like miso, natto, kimchi, and doenjang have never gone out of fashion and are embedded in daily eating culture, with national dietary guidelines actively encouraging their consumption. Germany and Eastern Europe have long traditions with sauerkraut and kefir that are seen as ordinary food rather than wellness trends. In the UK and US, fermented foods have been repackaged as a premium wellness category, which has driven both genuine interest in the science and a flood of poorly evidenced probiotic supplements.
top10.brit_take: Britain's been fermenting things for centuries — we just called it 'pickling' and kept quiet about it, and now suddenly it's a wellness trend at £6 a jar.

top10.claim: Anyone taking sertraline or fluoxetine warned to avoid common supplement
top10.verdict: This warning is well grounded and worth taking seriously. St John's Wort is the most likely supplement being referenced here, and its interaction with SSRIs like sertraline and fluoxetine is clinically documented — combining them raises the risk of serotonin syndrome, a potentially serious condition involving agitation, rapid heart rate, and high temperature. The NHS, WHO, and pharmacology literature all flag this interaction clearly. The word 'common' does the heavy lifting in the headline though — it's worth checking with a pharmacist about any supplement, not just one, when taking SSRIs.
top10.verdict_highlight: St John's Wort plus SSRIs is a real, documented risk
sources: NHS - St John's Wort interactions and safety guidance
JAMA - Herb-drug interactions in clinical practice
Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) - St John's Wort warning
top10.global_opinion: The UK's MHRA issued formal guidance on this interaction over two decades ago, and it is prominently flagged on NHS prescribing information — British GPs routinely ask patients about herbal supplements for exactly this reason. In Germany, where St John's Wort is actually licensed as a prescription antidepressant for mild depression, the interaction warning is built into the official prescribing literature and taken very seriously. In the US, the FDA and NIH both document the interaction clearly, though awareness among patients self-medicating with over-the-counter supplements remains inconsistent.
top10.brit_take: This one's genuinely worth a two-minute chat with your pharmacist — not because you've done anything wrong, but because herbal doesn't automatically mean harmless, and they won't judge you for asking.
